analysis.one_liner: Creates a simpler single-track consumer bankruptcy system letting people erase student loans and cut mortgage and car debts.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 18, 2024 with a single cosponsor and referred to two House committees, the bill died without a hearing or any vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the two-track consumer bankruptcy system with one simpler chapter, cutting paperwork and filing costs for people drowning in debt. It would let homeowners restructure mortgage debt, let borrowers cut car loans to the car's actual value, treat student loans like any other debt that can be wiped out, and close loopholes that let wealthy filers shield assets. It also voids forced-arbitration clauses in confirmed plans and strengthens protections against illegal debt collection.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and individuals in financial distress — typically from job loss, medical bills, or student debt — would benefit most. Filing would get cheaper and simpler, with a "minimum payment obligation" formula that requires little or nothing from lower-income households and discharges debt quickly. Homeowners could rewrite mortgage loans instead of facing foreclosure, car owners could pay only what the car is worth, student loan borrowers could discharge those debts on equal terms with other debt, and people could keep cars and rent-to-own goods needed for work and daily life. People behind on child support would get added notices and protections, and courts would collect data to expose racial and gender disparities in bankruptcy outcomes.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the dual Chapter 7/Chapter 13 system with a single 'Chapter 10' individual bankruptcy and repeals Chapter 13, streamlining paperwork and lowering the cost of filing for people who often have to save for months just to afford an attorney.

Sets a 'minimum payment obligation' that is zero or small for households earning near the state median (about 135% of median for one earner plus $15,000 per additional household member), and allows debtors to pay only what they reasonably can; debtors with a zero obligation get a discharge without even filing a plan.

Lets homeowners modify mortgage loans on any residence and cure defaults without penalty interest or late fees, a tool current law denies on primary homes and that the bill's findings link to unnecessary foreclosures.
Lets car buyers reduce auto loans to the vehicle's market value instead of paying more than the car is worth, and protects cars needed for work, school runs, and medical appointments.

Makes student loan debt dischargeable on equal terms with most other debt, addressing findings that nondischargeability has not lowered borrowing costs and that student debt is distorting labor and housing markets.

Caps repayment plans at 36 months, voids pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers in confirmed plans, restricts post-bankruptcy credit to court-approved loans with capped rates, and strengthens the discharge injunction so creditors and collectors cannot keep pursuing debts that were legally erased.

Treats rent-to-own customers as owners-in-progress who can keep needed household goods, and directs courts to collect data and provide judicial education aimed at reducing the racial and gender disparities the bill's findings say the current system produces.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors. Banks and credit card issuers would collect less on unsecured debts, since more debt would be discharged faster and with smaller required payments. Mortgage lenders and servicers would lose the ability to block restructuring of primary-residence loans; auto lenders would take losses when loans are cut to market value; private student loan companies would lose their special protection from discharge; and debt collectors would face stronger enforcement against pursuing discharged debts. Lenders might respond by pricing credit somewhat higher for everyone, and the retooled bankruptcy trustee system would be funded through restructured fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and consumer, mortgage, auto lenders

drawbacks.text: The bill is a near-total rewrite of consumer bankruptcy, and repealing Chapter 13 outright would eliminate a structure some debtors and secured creditors rely on, with transition rules (Section 502) that would create real adjustment costs for courts, trustees, and filers mid-case.

Creditors would recover less in bankruptcy, and an honest supporter should acknowledge that lenders may pass some of that loss back to borrowers through higher interest rates or tighter lending standards, affecting even people who never file.

The bill was never debated in committee, so its intricate machinery — a new security interest in favor of the trustee, court-approved post-petition credit with capped rates, and phased curtailment of avoidance actions — was never tested or amended by either party.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households in genuine financial distress, the benefits are large and concrete: cheaper filing, faster discharge, workable mortgages and car loans, and student debt treated like other debt. The costs fall on creditors and, indirectly, may show up as somewhat higher credit prices economy-wide — a tradeoff Congress's own 1978 framework already accepted in other forms. The bill's biggest weakness is procedural, not substantive: it was a sweeping rewrite introduced in the closing days of a Congress, with no hearing, no markup, and no chance for the courts, trustees, and lenders who would run the new system to shape it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the Congress, sent to two House committees, and neither one ever held a hearing, so it expired when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, joined by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2024 on December 18, 2024, just over two weeks before the 118th Congress expired.

The same day, the Speaker's office referred it to both the Judiciary Committee and the Financial Services Committee, splitting jurisdiction over a bill that touches bankruptcy law and consumer finance.
No committee took any further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors — banks, credit card issuers, mortgage and auto lenders, private student loan companies, and debt collectors — keep the existing bankruptcy system untouched, retaining the current limits on discharging student loans and restructuring home mortgages. Families in financial distress gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no partisan split is recorded; the bill's only supporters were two House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: Unsecured debts would be discharged faster and with smaller required payments, directly reducing what these lenders collect from distressed borrowers. Their interest runs against the debtors the bill would help.

The bill would let homeowners restructure primary-residence mortgages and cure defaults without penalty interest or late fees — a change current law forbids and that the industry relies on to keep home loans senior and unmodifiable.
Car loans could be cut to the vehicle's actual market value in bankruptcy, eliminating the 'pay more than the car is worth' dynamic the bill's findings describe.
Their loans would become dischargeable like ordinary debt, ending a special protection Congress granted in 2005 that the bill's findings say never lowered borrowers' financing costs.
Stronger discharge-injunction enforcement, codebtor stays, and a ban on post-discharge pursuit of rent-to-own property would sharply limit collection on erased debts.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy trustees and consumer bankruptcy attorneys
industries.note: Simpler, cheaper filings would let more distressed people afford counsel and let attorneys be paid through plans, but streamlined no-payment cases and reduced paperwork would mean less billable work in routine cases; trustee compensation would be restructured under Title IV.
The bill would strip them of property interests in rent-to-own goods, cap what customers owe if they keep the items, and bar collection after discharge.
